title: The Laplace Probe
question: Can one measured area tell us where a signal lives?

blocks.text: Every time we solved something, we *guessed* $e^{st}$, plugged it in, and prayed. Now add gravity, a starting height, a controller… my notebook is on fire.
When I build stuff, the trick is always to turn a hard job into an easy one. Hard: calculus with slopes of slopes. Easy: plain algebra with $+$, $-$, $\times$, $\div$.
So we need a machine that eats a curve and spits out something where slopes turn into multiplication? Does that exist?

It does, and we can build it from things we already own. Here's the idea. Take any **signal**, any curve that changes over time, $f(t)$. Multiply it by a **probe**, the exponential $e^{-st}$ from Chapter 4 (for positive $s$ it shrinks). Then measure the **total area** under the product (Chapter 3's accumulated area), all the way out to $t = \infty$.

That's it. A number $s$ goes in, an area comes out. Try different $s$ values and you get a whole new curve $F(s)$. That curve is the **Laplace transform** of $f$: a fingerprint of the signal. Two different (reasonable) signals never share the same $F(s)$, which is why we'll be able to look answers up backwards later.
Why *that* curve? Why not a bump, or a sine?

Two reasons, and I can count them on my fingers. One: it's Chapter 4's special curve. Its slope is just $-s$ times itself, so when slopes show up, they'll turn into multiplying by $s$. Two: it's the exact opposite of the $e^{st}$ we kept guessing. Hold it against $e^{at}$ and the two cancel when $s = a$.
We'll watch the cancelling in the next section, and the slopes in the next chapter.

blocks.q: Take the simplest signal, a step: $f(t) = 1$ forever. As we make $s$ **bigger**, what happens to the area under $1 \cdot e^{-st}$?

options.why: A bigger $s$ makes the probe die out *faster*, so there's less of it.
Right. A bigger $s$ squashes the probe faster, so there's less area. In fact the area is exactly $1/s$ (we'll prove it when we build our table).
The probe's shape depends on $s$: bigger $s$ means a quicker drop, so a smaller area.

blocks.text: Probe the step at s = {scrub|s}: the area is 1 ÷ {calc|s} = {calc|F}. Double s and the area halves.

Sweep $s$ in the widget and the dots trace out exactly that $1/s$. Try the other signals too. A growing signal $e^{0.5t}$ only has a finite area when the probe shrinks **faster** than the signal grows, that is when $s > 0.5$. Below that, the area runs off to infinity. The wiggle $\sin 2t$ fails differently: at $s = 0$ its area just sloshes back and forth between 0 and 1 (Chapter 3's negative area cancelling the positive), and never settles on one number.

blocks.title: An endless area that stops growing

blocks.text: Wait. The probe goes on forever. How can forever have a finite area?

Because most of forever is almost nothing. Each extra second adds less than the one before. After one second the area under $e^{-t}$ is already 63% of the total (Chapter 3's τ ruler again). After five, it's past 99%.
Stop adding the area of $e^{-t}$ at t = {scrub|T} s and you already have {calc|A}. Everything after that adds only {calc|left}.
So forever is fine, as long as the tail gets thin fast enough. That's exactly what the probe is for.
The total area must settle to a finite value, so that each $s$ gets one number. If the probe fades too slowly, the area keeps growing and that $s$ has no answer.
We're only using real $s$ for now. Complex $s$ comes in a minute, and it's where the magic is.

sections.title: The transform screams where the signal lives

blocks.text: Let's look closer at $f(t) = e^{at}$. Probe it with $e^{-st}$ and the product is $e^{(a-s)t}$, a plain exponential. As long as $s > a$ it fades, and its area is $\frac{1}{s-a}$ (we'll derive it properly when we build our table in the next chapter).
As $s$ gets close to $a$ the number goes **huge**! At $s = a$ the probe exactly cancels the growth, the product is flat forever, and the area is infinite.
So the transform **blows up exactly at the** $s$ **where the signal lives**. If you gave me only $F(s)$, I could find the signal's $a$ by looking for where it explodes.
Signal $e^{at}$ with a = {scrub|a|out}, probe s = {scrub|s}: the product fades at s − a = {calc|gap} per second, so its area is {calc|F}. {calc|verdict}
It's like a smoke alarm. Walk $s$ towards $a$ and it gets louder and louder. Step onto $a$ and it never stops.

Now make $s$ complex, $s = \sigma + i\omega$, just like our spinning numbers from Chapter 5. Take the spring's spinner from Chapter 6, $e^{2it}$ (half of its twin pair), as the signal. The probe $e^{-st}$ shrinks it (that's the left-right part, $\sigma$) **and spins it backwards** (that's the up-down part, $\omega$). Below, the product's little pieces of area are added up head-to-tail as arrows, one arrow for every quarter second. Watch the running total.

When the probe spins at exactly 2, the signal stops spinning, all the pieces point the same way and the total is as big as it gets: $1/\sigma$, which runs off to infinity as σ shrinks to 0. When they don't match, the arrows curl around and cancel out.

Same lesson, one dimension up: the transform explodes at the complex $s$ where the signal lives. That's why from now on we'll draw every $s$ on a map with $\sigma$ across and $\omega$ up. Our "map of $s$" from Chapter 6 finally gets its grown-up name: the **s-plane**.

items.def: The map of complex numbers $s = \sigma + i\omega$. Left means shrinking, right means growing, up and down means spinning. Every signal $e^{st}$ lives at one point on it, and its transform explodes there.

items: The Laplace transform is a **probe**: multiply by $e^{-st}$ and measure the total area. $F(s) = \int_0^\infty f(t)e^{-st}dt$.
It **explodes exactly where the signal lives**: $e^{at}$ gives $1/(s-a)$, which blows up at $s = a$. For complex $s$ the probe unspins spinning signals. We plot all of this on the **s-plane**.
An area over *forever* can still be finite, as long as the tail thins out fast enough. If the probe fades more slowly than the signal grows, that $s$ has no transform at all.

items.q: The transform of $e^{3t}$ is $\frac{1}{s-3}$. Theo plugs in $s = 1$ and gets $-\frac12$. What went wrong?

options.text: At $s = 1$ the area never settles, so there is no transform there
options.why: The product is $e^{3t}e^{-t} = e^{2t}$, which grows forever. The formula only holds where the probe wins, for $s > 3$.
A positive signal times a positive probe can't have a negative area. The formula is being used where it doesn't hold.
$\frac{1}{s+3}$ belongs to $e^{-3t}$. The formula is fine; the $s$ isn't.
It explodes at $s = -4$, so the signal lives at $e^{-4t}$. The 5 on top is its size.
A growing $e^{4t}$ would explode at $s = +4$. This one explodes at $s = -4$.
Wiggles need a pair of complex explosion points, a spinner and its mirror twin. Here there's a single real one at $-4$.

items.q: Where on the s-plane does the transform of the spinner $e^{2it}$ explode?

options.why: The spinner is $e^{st}$ with $s = 2i$, so that's where it lives. There the probe unspins it exactly.
That's where $e^{2t}$ lives: a growing signal with no spin at all.
That's the step's home. The spinner's explosion point is up at $2i$.

blocks.text: Theo: "So the probe tells us *where* a signal lives. But we wanted slopes to turn into multiplication. **What does the probe do to a slope?**"

probe.title: The probe
probe.plotAria: The signal, the probe and their product over time, with the area under the product shaded.
probe.fAria: Traced values of the total area F against s, one dot for each s you tried.
probe.help: Move s and let go (or pause after the arrow keys): the area is measured and a dot is added to the F(s) plot. After 5 dots, spread across different s, you can reveal the formula.
probe.finite: At s = {s} the total area is {F}.
probe.infinite: Here the probe doesn't shrink faster than the signal. The area never settles: it's infinite.
probe.sloshes: Here the area never settles. It keeps sloshing back and forth, so this s has no single answer.
probe.window: The picture shows the first 8 s; the rest adds {rest}.

explode.title: Where does it blow up?
explode.prodAria: The product of e to the a t and the probe, with its area shaded.
explode.fAria: The transform 1 over s minus a, with a vertical line where it blows up.
explode.never: s is at or below a: the product never shrinks, so the area is infinite.
explode.close: Getting close to a: the area is {F} and climbing!
explode.calm: Far from a: a nice finite area.
explode.window: The picture shows only the first 10 s; {pct}% of the area is still to come.

unspin.title: A probe that unspins
unspin.path: running total (one arrow per ¼ s)
unspin.plotAria: The running total of the complex area drawn as a path in the plane, heading towards its final value.
unspin.matched: Spins matched! Every piece points the same way. The total is {m} = 1/⁠σ, and it heads to infinity as σ → 0.
unspin.spinning: The pieces curl around and mostly cancel. The total stays small.

scream.none: It never fades, so there is no finite area at all.
